Semiconductor Supply Chain Knowledge Graph for Equity Research

Semiconductor Supply Chain Knowledge Graph for Equity Research

Knowledge-Based Systems · Term Project 2 (individual): clusters, relationship prediction and question answering on the Team 2 graph · Korea University

Who supplies, makes, uses and owns what in the chip industry. Relations were extracted by LLMs from the Wikipedia articles and SEC annual filings of 50 semiconductor and AI-hardware companies, then matched to canonical entities, merged across sources and checked against the CSET ETO Chip Explorer. Phase 2 adds what the graph implies but does not state: companies grouped by what they make, who they trade with and where they sit in the value chain, and predicted customer and supplier relations with the evidence path behind each, always shown apart from the stated ones.

    Relations

    Confidence: HIGH when at least two independent publishers state the relation (all filings of one company count as one publisher, Wikipedia as another), MEDIUM for a single publisher, LOW for unresolved conflicts and relations that only held in the past or for a limited scope. Support (0–1) adds up the evidence from independent publishers. It ranks relations; it is not a probability. Click a row to read the evidence.
    Analysis tools

    Computed from the graph in your browser. The graph only holds what the 128 source documents state, and it finds about half of the inputs in the ETO reference, so a missing link does not mean there is none. Links show that a dependency exists, not how large it is.

    Companies by cluster

    Thick arrows: the production sequence. Click a company for its partners and predictions, or a stage for the supply links in and out of it. Drag to pan, Ctrl + scroll to zoom.

    Recall against ETO

    Share of the 128 company–input pairs that ETO lists for 28 of the 50 companies that the graph contains, judged pair by pair by gpt-oss-120b. Strict counts an exact or more specific offering; graded gives half credit when the graph only names a broader category. Whiskers: company-level bootstrap 95% intervals. Both graph versions were judged with the same protocol.

    Confidence against ETO

    Share of the graph's product families for these companies that ETO also lists. ETO is incomplete, so an unconfirmed family is not necessarily wrong; the comparison between groups is the point. Measured on the original graph (v1) with the earlier judge.

    Precision by source

    Is the relation stated in its evidence? Dark bars: 79 audited relations (LLM labels, every rejection reviewed by hand). Light bars: 511 relations checked by gpt-oss-120b, which agreed with the audit labels at κ 0.45. Both measured on the original graph (v1); on the reviewed graph the same check finds 81% overall.

    Audit (79)LLM check (511)

    Precision by relation

    LLM check on 511 relations, about 70 per type. Stage relations are left out because the checker judged them against the text although they are type classifications (audit: 8 of 9 correct). Measured on the original graph (v1).

    Question answering: held-out test

    Who sells what to whom: coverage

    Predicted relations: how often the true partner is found

    What each part of the recommender adds

    Mean reciprocal rank (1 = the hidden partner ranked first, 0.5 = second). Hybrid = reciprocal-rank fusion of peers, product peers and popularity, then the product gate. Remove one part to see what it carries; stage and ecosystem were tested as extra parts and left out because they lowered the score.

    Roles and stages against ETO

    38 companies of the graph have an ETO label. Role and stage from products are compared with what ETO says each company provides; the Phase 1 stage labels are the baseline. Bars: share correct where the method gives an answer; the count shows how many of the 38 it covers.

    Limits of these numbers

    • Version 2 is the reviewed graph: 143 flagged error cases were checked against the sources, 50 claims corrected and 117 set aside, and 244 missing evidence statements recovered. The result has 2,988 relations instead of 3,140. The review was model-assisted, not expert gold.
    • The precision gain (76% to 81%) is measured after fixing errors that earlier checks had found, partly on the same sampled relations, so it is not a held-out test of the method.
    • The pairwise ETO judge finds every hand-labelled exact match (17 of 17) but also accepts 7 pairs that people marked as only partial, so true strict recall is likely lower, around 40%. Recall against ETO did not change between versions.
    • ETO's reference is mostly equipment makers (104 of 128 pairs are tools) and has no rows for fabless and analog companies, so recall describes a narrow slice of the graph. Three companies hold 72 of the 128 pairs, which is why the intervals are wide.
    • The support score ranks relations but is not calibrated. The HIGH / MEDIUM label is the better signal.
    Graph v2 (reviewed) by Team 2: 50 Wikipedia articles and 78 SEC 10-K / 20-F filings. Phase 2 (clusters, value chain, predicted relations) is computed from that graph without new extraction; predicted relations are hypotheses, not facts. Reference data: CSET Emerging Technology Observatory, Chip Explorer and Supply Chain Explorer (CC BY-NC 4.0), used for a non-commercial course project. Value-chain stages follow CSIS, "Simplified Depiction of the Semiconductor Value Chain". Relations extracted by LLMs may contain errors; check the evidence.
